<reason>Side B (CON) built the cleaner route to victory by attacking the motion as written—the conjunctive "only when, all three" gate—and forcing PRO into a dilemma it never escaped: either "stronger plans" mean real obligations that block the low-risk jazz bar for no reason, or they mean describing existing services, in which case the gate is ornamental friction. PRO defended competently, insisting planning and enforcement are complementary (readiness vs. delivery) and that someone must bear the risk before enforcement catches up, but its own answers steadily shrank the motion's work: "merely listing a subway prevents nothing by itself," the real protection is staff directing departures (a conduct condition), employer-funded taxis can fill the transport gap (which happens without a gate), and an unresolved transit gap means "denied" (putting the agency-veto on the record). B tracked each concession, answered A's pressure questions honestly and directly with A1/A2, neutralized the "moves it next door" worry with a dispersal-radius condition, and closed by crystallizing the clash rather than recapping. A's best surviving point—advance verification of cleanup staffing is not nothing—was not fully killed by B's "rota on a page" reply, and B's clipped opening is a small execution cost, which keeps this a clear but competitive win rather than dominant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Pressure Q1/Q2 and follow-up in B4.6–B4.8: after forcing PRO to admit the transit paragraph "prevents nothing by itself" and that the extension is "denied" when the agency stays silent, B showed every protective mechanism PRO named was a behavioural condition outside the plan wrapper, leaving the gate doing only two things—blocking venues for city failures and demanding documents where nothing needs adding.</best_rebuttal>
